title: Oil prices plunge as Iran says Strait 'open'
content:
**Headline:** Global Markets Breathe a Sigh of Relief as Iran Announces Reopening of Strait of Hormuz, Oil Prices Plummet

In a move that has sent shockwaves of relief through global markets, Iran has announced that the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for international oil trade, will be "completely open" to commercial ships for the remainder of the ceasefire. This declaration has triggered a sharp decline in oil prices, with Brent crude plummeting to $88 per barrel, down from $98 earlier in the day.

The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf to the Arabian Sea, is a vital artery for the global oil trade, with approximately one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passing through it. The waterway's closure, which was effectively shut down by Iran following US and Israeli military strikes in late February, had drastically reduced the global supply of oil and gas, causing prices to skyrocket. Prior to the conflict, Brent crude was trading at under $70 per barrel, but it surged to over $100 and peaked at $119 per barrel in March.

US President Donald Trump has welcomed Iran's announcement, taking to social media to express his appreciation. However, maritime groups, including the international shipping body BIMCO, are exercising caution, advising operators to remain vigilant due to ongoing risks. Jakob Larsen, BIMCO's chief safety and security officer, warned that the status of mine threats in the area remains unclear, and shipping companies should consider avoiding the region.

The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is also seeking clarification on the details of Iran's commitment to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez stated that the organization is verifying the announcement to ensure compliance with freedom of navigation for all merchant vessels and secure passage using the established traffic separation scheme.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz has significant implications for global markets, with the major US stock indices rising in early trading. The S&P 500, Nasdaq, and Dow Jones Industrial Average all experienced gains, while European shares also rallied, with the Cac index in Paris and Dax in Frankfurt climbing by over 2%. The FTSE 100 in London rose by approximately 0.5%.

However, the impact of the conflict on global supply chains will likely be felt for months to come. Professor ManMohan Sodhi of the Bayes Business School noted that even if a longer-term peace deal is reached, consumers will continue to feel the pressure as supply chains take time to clear. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has not only affected oil prices but also led to a shortage of fertilizers, used by farmers, which could result in higher food prices.

As the world watches the developments in the region, the question remains whether the current ceasefire will hold and lead to a lasting peace. The halt to weeks of fighting has brought relief to Lebanon, but ensuring its sustainability will be a challenging task. With the global economy still reeling from the effects of the conflict, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz offers a glimmer of hope for a return to stability in the region.

title: Ceasefire with Israel brings respite to Lebanon, but obstacles to peace remain
content:
**"Fragile Calm: Lebanon Breathes a Sigh of Relief as Ceasefire Takes Hold, But Hurdles to Lasting Peace Remain"**

In the early hours of the morning, the streets of Beirut erupted in a cacophony of gunfire and fireworks, marking the beginning of a tenuous 10-day ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia Muslim militia and political party. The agreement, brokered by US President Donald Trump, has brought a measure of respite to a nation reeling from six weeks of brutal conflict, which has left over 2,100 people dead and more than a million displaced.

As the ceasefire took hold, jubilant crowds gathered on roads leading to southern Lebanon, the heartland of Hezbollah, waving the group's yellow flag and playing revolutionary music. However, the celebratory atmosphere belies the daunting challenges that lie ahead. Many of the displaced are hesitant to return to their homes, fearing that the damage is too extensive or that they may not be allowed to reoccupy their properties due to the ongoing Israeli occupation of some areas.

In the southern suburbs of Beirut, known as Dahieh, the streets remained relatively quiet, a testament to the devastating impact of the war. The area has been pounded by Israeli forces, leaving many residential buildings in ruins. The city's waterfront, where hundreds of displaced families have been living in makeshift tents, was also subdued, with many expressing fears about returning to their homes.

The ceasefire agreement has raised more questions than answers, leaving many to wonder if this is merely a temporary reprieve or a genuine step towards lasting peace. The deal does not address the withdrawal of Israeli troops from southern Lebanon, sparking concerns that parts of the country may remain under occupation. Furthermore, the issue of Hezbollah's weapons, which has long been a contentious point, remains unresolved. The US, Israel, and many Lebanese have called for the group's disarmament, but Hezbollah has refused to discuss the matter, with a high-ranking member, Wafiq Safa, stating that the group would "never, ever" disarm.

The relationship between Hezbollah and Iran is also a significant hurdle to overcome. Safa described the bond between the two as "two souls in one body," emphasizing the deep-seated ties between the group and its patron. The Lebanese government, which has limited influence over Hezbollah, has warned that disarmament cannot be achieved through force and would require negotiations with the group. However, given Iran's significant role in the equation, it is likely that any decision regarding the future of Hezbollah's weapons will be made in Tehran, rather than Beirut.

The ceasefire agreement also leaves open the possibility of Israel continuing to attack Lebanon, citing security concerns, which could potentially plunge the country back into chaos. This has raised concerns that the situation may revert to the pre-conflict status quo, where Israel carried out regular attacks on targets and individuals allegedly linked to Hezbollah.

Despite these challenges, there are signs of diplomatic progress, with some vessels from Iranian ports reportedly crossing a US blockade line in the Gulf of Oman. The price of Brent crude has also fallen, and UK petrol and diesel prices have begun to decrease after 46 consecutive days of rises. However, it remains to be seen whether these developments will be enough to prevent a return to war.

As the international community watches with bated breath, one thing is clear: the path to lasting peace in Lebanon will be long and arduous, requiring careful navigation of the complex web of interests and alliances that have fueled the conflict. The fragile calm that has descended upon the nation is a welcome respite, but it is only the first step towards a more lasting and equitable solution.

title: Thousands celebrate open-air Mass with Pope Leo in Cameroon - in pictures
content:
**Pope Leo XIV Brings Message of Hope to Cameroon: Tens of Thousands Gather for Open-Air Mass**

In a remarkable display of faith and unity, over 120,000 people congregated at the Japoma Stadium in Douala, Cameroon, to participate in an open-air Mass led by Pope Leo XIV. This historic event marked the largest gathering during the Pope's 11-day Africa tour, which has already taken him to Algeria and will conclude in Equatorial Guinea.

Upon his arrival in Douala on Friday, Pope Leo XIV reiterated his message of peace, a theme that has been at the forefront of his visit to Cameroon. The country's Anglophone region has been plagued by a decade-long rebellion, and the Pope's words of encouragement and unity were eagerly received by the jubilant crowds.

As the Pope made his way to the stadium in the Popemobile, he was greeted by throngs of people who had waited for hours, some even camping outside the premises overnight, to secure a prime spot for the occasion. The atmosphere was electric, with people of all ages, including members of the priesthood, braving the heat to participate in the Mass.

In his address, Pope Leo XIV focused on spiritual matters, urging young people to harness their talents and support their communities. He also cautioned against the dangers of abuse and violence, emphasizing the importance of rejecting temptations that can lead to corruption and harm to society. "Reject every form of abuse or violence, which deceives by promising easy gains but hardens the heart and makes it insensitive," the Pope said. "Do not let yourselves be corrupted by temptations that waste your energies and do not serve the progress of society."

The crowd was deeply moved by the Pope's words, with many attendees expressing their gratitude for the opportunity to see and listen to him. As they raised their hands in prayer, some used umbrellas and books to shield themselves from the sun, while others wiped sweat from their faces. The worship took many forms, with some clasping their hands together and others prostrating themselves in devotion.

In addition to the Mass, Pope Leo XIV also visited the St Paul Catholic Hospital in Douala, where he continued to spread his message of hope and peace. As he prepares to travel to Angola and eventually Equatorial Guinea, the Pope's visit to Cameroon has been a powerful reminder of the importance of faith and unity in the face of adversity.

The Pope's 11-day Africa tour, which began in Algeria, marks a significant milestone in his efforts to engage with the continent and promote peace and understanding. As he continues his journey, the world watches with interest, eager to see the impact of his message on the people and communities he encounters.
